title_en: Ge Liang v. Li Hui et al. — dispute over a house sales contract
ruling_gist_en: The determination of the validity of a housing sales contract involving 'predatory lending' should not be conclusively deemed valid solely based on a notarized authorization document. Instead, the true intent of the parties must be ascertained, and the validity of the concealed civil juristic act should be comprehensively evaluated and determined in accordance with the law.
keywords_en: Civil; Dispute over housing sales contract; First instance; Primary People's Court; Shanghai; Natural person; Civil Code; Validity of contract; True expression of intent; Malicious collusion; Predatory lending; Housing sale; Mortgage loan; Notarized authorization; Debt repayment with property; Good faith; Contract dispute; Sales contract; Mortgage; Lawsuit against Li Hui et al. for housing sales contract dispute
full_text_en:
Ge Liang v. Li Hui, et al. — Dispute over Housing Sales Contract

【Ruling Summary】

In determining the validity of a housing sales contract involving "loan-sharking tactics" (taolu dai), a court should not simply deem the contract valid based solely on a notarized power of attorney. It must ascertain the true intentions of the parties and comprehensively evaluate the validity of the concealed civil juristic act in accordance with the law.

Plaintiff: Ge Liang, male, born November 13, 1981, residing in Yangpu District, Shanghai.

Defendant: Li Hui, male, born January 8, 1962, residing in Jing'an District, Shanghai.

Third Party: Li Shuai, male, born December 6, 1967, residing in Jing'an District, Shanghai.

Third Party: Xiao Zhongxiang, female, born August 15, 1980, residing in Songjiang District, Shanghai.

Plaintiff Ge Liang filed a lawsuit with the Yangpu District People's Court of Shanghai against Defendant Li Hui, and Third Parties Li Shuai and Xiao Zhongxiang, regarding a dispute over a housing sales contract.

Plaintiff Ge Liang alleged: In October 2014, Plaintiff entered into a loan and mortgage contract with Third Party Xiao Zhongxiang, agreeing to borrow RMB 1,200,000 from Xiao, and mortgaged the property to Xiao Zhongxiang. On April 30, 2015, without Plaintiff's knowledge, Third Party Li Shuai, acting as Plaintiff's agent, entered into a housing sales contract with Defendant Li Hui, selling the disputed property to Defendant at a price below market value. Defendant is the elder brother of Third Party Li Shuai. The contract transfer price was RMB 1,500,000. On May 18, 2015, Defendant was registered as the title holder. Plaintiff never received any payment or other consideration whatsoever. Plaintiff did sign a corresponding power of attorney when executing the loan and mortgage contract, but Plaintiff was unaware of this because at that time he was only seeking a loan and had no intention of selling the house, and he had been paying interest on the loan. The contact telephone numbers of Xiao Zhongxiang and Li Shuai on the housing sales contract were the same, which also proves that the third parties, on behalf of the lender, were jointly handling this matter. Therefore, Defendant and the third parties maliciously colluded to damage Plaintiff's legitimate rights and interests, and the disputed housing sales contract should be declared invalid. Accordingly, Plaintiff requests: 1. A declaration that the "Shanghai Real Estate Sales Contract" numbered 2211220 is invalid, and that the property located at Room ×-×, Building ×, Shiguang Yicun be restored to Plaintiff's name; 2. An order that Defendant bear the litigation costs of this case.

Defendant Li Hui and Third Party Li Shuai argued: Plaintiff Ge Liang, as the borrower, should act in good faith. Plaintiff was aware of the mortgage and had provided the property deed and password to the third party at that time. Plaintiff personally signed the power of attorney before the notary public, and the notarial certificate stated that the sale price of the house should not be less than RMB 1,500,000, reflecting Plaintiff's true intention. Third Party Xiao Zhongxiang had a non-local household registration, and the house might be subject to purchase restrictions, so Defendant purchased it instead. Although Defendant and the third party are biological brothers, this does not prove malicious collusion. The full purchase price of RMB 1,500,000 was paid by Defendant to Xiao Zhongxiang to offset the loan principal of RMB 1,200,000 and interest. Court enforcement is not the only means; other methods to realize the claim were also available. The sale of the disputed property did not require compulsory execution through the People's Court. As a fully authorized agent, Li Shuai had the right to choose the fastest way to handle the matter. Defendant requests that the court protect his lawful interests.

Third Party Xiao Zhongxiang stated: She disagreed with Plaintiff Ge Liang's claims. The "Shanghai Real Estate Sales Contract" did not meet the statutory conditions for invalidity; the contract was lawfully formed and legally valid. Xiao Zhongxiang paid the full loan amount of RMB 1,200,000 to Plaintiff on October 20, 2014. Prior to the loan, Plaintiff had agreed with Xiao Zhongxiang that if the loan was not repaid upon maturity, the house would be transferred to satisfy the debt at a price of RMB 1,500,000. Upon expiration of the loan term, Xiao Zhongxiang repeatedly sought repayment from Plaintiff but was unsuccessful. Ultimately, at Xiao Zhongxiang's instruction, Li Shuai, relying on the legally valid notarized power of attorney, re-executed the "Shanghai Real Estate Sales Contract" with Defendant Li Hui in accordance with the original contract terms, and completed the transfer procedures lawfully. The transfer of the house was based on the contractual agreement and Plaintiff's true intention, and the agency procedures were complete. The contract was lawfully established and legally valid. Plaintiff's claim of being completely unaware was inconsistent with the facts of this case. His statement that he "did not receive any payment or other consideration" actually proves that Xiao Zhongxiang considered that upon completion of the transfer, the consideration for the house was deemed to offset the portion of the loan that Plaintiff should have repaid. Consequently, the debt of RMB 1,500,000 between Plaintiff and Xiao Zhongxiang was extinguished. Plaintiff had known since the time of the loan the roles of Defendant and the third parties in the legal relationship and had foreseen the legal consequences of default. There was no malicious collusion. Plaintiff's request to invalidate the contract and restore the property registration would directly render it difficult for Xiao Zhongxiang to realize her claim. She requested the court to reject Plaintiff's claims in accordance with the law.

The Yangpu District People's Court of Shanghai found the following facts at first instance:

On October 20, 2014, Plaintiff Ge Liang (borrower/mortgagor, Party A) and Third Party Xiao Zhongxiang (lender/mortgagee, Party B) entered into a Loan and Mortgage Contract. Article 1 stipulated that Party A borrowed RMB 1,200,000 in total from Party B. Article 3 stipulated a loan term of two months, from October 20, 2014 to December 19, 2014. Article 4 stipulated that the monthly interest rate for the loan was four times the benchmark lending rate of the People's Bank of China for the same period, with interest to be paid together with principal upon maturity. Article 6 stipulated that Party A would mortgage a property over which he had lawful disposal rights to Party B as security for the repayment of the debt under this contract. The specific details of the mortgaged property were: Property address: Room ×-×, Building ×, Shiguang Yicun, Yangpu District, Shanghai; Property type: residential; Building area: 71.84 square meters; Property value: RMB 1,500,000 (negotiated price). Party A had lawful disposal rights over the above property as collateral. In the afternoon of the same day, Ge Liang and Defendant Li Hui entered into a "Shanghai Real Estate Sales Contract" (online signing), contract number 2101100, under which Ge Liang sold the property located at Room ×-×, Building ×, Shiguang Yicun, Yangpu District, Shanghai to Li Hui at a transfer price of RMB 1,500,000. Both parties agreed that Ge Liang would vacate the property before January 19, 2015, and notify Li Hui for inspection and handover, and jointly apply to the Real Estate Transaction Center for transfer registration. Li Hui was to pay 80% of the total purchase price, i.e., RMB 1,200,000, as a deposit before October 20, 2014, which would be offset against the purchase price upon payment of the balance, and pay RMB 300,000 before January 19, 2015.

On October 20, 2014, Plaintiff Ge Liang, as the principal, executed a Power of Attorney designating Third Party Li Shuai as the agent. The Power of Attorney stated: I. Scope of Authority: Because the principal is unable to personally handle the matters concerning the lease or sale (at a price not less than RMB 1,500,000) of the property registered in the principal's name located at Room ×-×, Building ×, Shiguang Yicun, Yangpu District, Shanghai, the principal hereby appoints the agent Li Shuai to act on behalf of the principal within the scope of authority to handle all matters listed in the appendix below. The term of authority is from December 20, 2014 to December 19, 2015, and the agent has no right to sub-delegate. The principal acknowledges and accepts all legal acts performed by the agent within the scope of authority and the legal consequences arising therefrom. Appendix: 1. Execute deposit agreements; 2. Execute, modify, and rescind real estate sales contracts, and, if necessary, handle contract cancellation procedures; 3. Handle notarization of the sales contract and obtain the notarial certificate; 4. Handle real estate transfer registration, sign commitment letters and other documents required by the transaction center; 5. Handle loan repayment and insurance surrender procedures, obtain certificates of mortgage rights, debt clearance certificates, and other deregistration materials, and handle the deregistration of real estate mortgage registration; 6. Handle matters related to re-mortgage; 7. Assist the buyer in handling mortgage loan procedures and sign relevant documents; 8. Collect the purchase price (either the principal's or agent's account), and issue receipts; 9. Obtain original purchase documents from the Real Estate Transaction Center, Taxation Bureau, developer, and other relevant departments; 10. Handle property handover procedures (including water, electricity, gas, fixed telephone, broadband cancellation, transfer, and related matters, as well as property management handover procedures); 11. Apply for replacement of lost Real Estate Ownership Certificate and password slip; 12. Handle procedures for moving out household registration from the above property; 13. Handle price verification, tax review (including signing tax-related commitment documents), and pay relevant taxes; 14. Execute lease contracts, lease agreements, handle lease registration filing procedures, and obtain the above real estate registration certificate; 15. Handle matters concerning modification and rescission of lease contracts, collect rent (including deposits), pay liquidated damages (if any), and cancel lease registration filing; 16. Handle other related matters in the process of leasing or selling the real estate. On October 31, 2014, the Baoshan Notary Public Office of Shanghai issued Notarial Certificate (2014) Hu Bao Zheng Jing Zi No. 13988, and Ge Liang signed the Power of Attorney.

On October 31, 2014, Notarial Certificate (2014) Hu Bao Zheng Zi No. 13987 stated: Party A (borrower, mortgagor) Ge Liang, Party B (lender, mortgagee) Xiao Zhongxiang. Notarial matter: Notarization of a creditor's rights instrument with compulsory enforcement effect. The notarization was to confer compulsory enforcement effect on the Loan and Mortgage Contract signed by Ge Liang and Xiao Zhongxiang.

On April 30, 2015, Third Party Li Shuai, as the authorized agent of Ge Liang (seller, Party A), and his elder brother, Defendant Li Hui (buyer, Party B), entered into a "Shanghai Real Estate Sales Contract" (contract number 2211220, online signing date March 21, 2015). Under this contract, the property owned by the Plaintiff at Room ×-×, Building ×, Shiguang Yicun, Yangpu District, Shanghai was sold to Li Hui. The building area was 71.84 square meters, the transfer price was RMB 1,500,000, with no loan, full payment was to be made before May 10, 2015, and both parties confirmed that they would jointly apply to the Real Estate Transaction Center for transfer registration before June 20, 2015. The contract contained no provisions regarding the time for vacating the property, delayed vacating, delayed payment, or handling of the mortgage. After the relevant mortgage discharge procedures were completed for the disputed property, on May 18, 2015, the Shanghai Real Estate Register approved Li Hui as the title holder of the property.

On November 24, 2015, the First Residents' Committee of Shiguang Yicun, Yinhang Subdistrict, Yangpu District, Shanghai issued a certificate stating that, according to the household registration booklet, residents of Room ×, Building ×, Shiguang Yicun, Hou Linsheng and Xia Yuedi had been living there since August 4, 1998, and Hou Xuejing had been living there since January 5, 2012.

On March 29, 30, and 31, 2015, payments of RMB 5,000, RMB 6,000, RMB 10,000, and RMB 6,000 were made from an Alipay account under the name Hou Xuejing (account number 13×××××××03) to Third Party Xiao Zhongxiang's Industrial and Commercial Bank of China card number 6222 ×××× ×××× ×××× 5451, with the description indicating repayment on behalf of Plaintiff Ge Liang.

At 14:28 on December 24, 2015, Hou Xuejing reported a police incident, alleging a property dispute at Room ×, Building ×, Shiguang Yicun, with the conflict escalating, and stating that the other party was damaging property. The police were requested to handle the matter. On January 19, 2016, Hou Linsheng, Xia Yuedi, and Hou Xuejing moved out of the disputed property.

It was also found that in related case (2016) Hu 01 Min Zhong No. 1074 being heard by the court, Third Parties Li Shuai and Xiao Zhongxiang had acted as agents in the sale of properties. In that case, Huang Niangui and others had entrusted Xiao Zhongxiang through a notarized power of attorney to handle the sale of a property, and on December 10, 2014, Xiao Zhongxiang sold the property on behalf of Huang Niangui and others to Li Shuai.

During the trial, the court commissioned Shanghai Zhongyuan Property Consultancy Co., Ltd. and Shanghai Ruifeng Investment Advisory Co., Ltd. to appraise the disputed property. Shanghai Zhongyuan Property Consultancy Co., Ltd. issued an appraisal opinion stating that the objective and reasonable market price of the appraised property at the end of April 2015 was RMB 29,000-30,000 per square meter. Shanghai Ruifeng Investment Advisory Co., Ltd. issued an appraisal opinion stating that the unit price of the disputed property in April 2015 was RMB 29,000-31,000 per square meter.

The Yangpu District People's Court of Shanghai held at first instance as follows:

The focus of the dispute in this case is the validity of the real estate sales contract for the disputed property entered into by Third Party Li Shuai in the name of Plaintiff Ge Liang with Defendant Li Hui.

First, the sale of the property by Third Party Li Shuai to realize the debt violated legal prohibitions. After the debt became due and the mortgagee had not been satisfied, the mortgagee and the mortgagor may agree to obtain the mortgaged property through a discounted price. However, the exercise of the mortgage right must follow statutory procedures, either through an agreement with the mortgagor or through court proceedings. The mortgagee has no right to dispose of the mortgaged property without authorization. If the mortgage contract stipulates that upon the maturity of the debt and failure of the mortgagee to be satisfied, the ownership of the mortgaged property shall transfer to the mortgagee, such a provision is void. When Plaintiff Ge Liang and Third Party Xiao Zhongxiang executed the real estate mortgage loan contract, they also entered into a "Shanghai Real Estate Sales Contract" with Defendant Li Hui, and then went to the notary office to obtain a "Notarial Certificate of Creditor's Rights Instrument with Compulsory Enforcement Effect" and a "Notarial Power of Attorney." Although the mortgage loan contract did not expressly state that if Ge Liang failed to repay the loan at maturity, the mortgaged property would belong to Xiao Zhongxiang, the condition for Xiao Zhongxiang to lend money to Ge Liang was that Ge Liang had to issue a power of attorney granting Li Shuai the authority to, among other things, sign a real estate sales contract, collect the purchase price, and handle property title transfer procedures. In other words, Xiao Zhongxiang must have the right to dispose of the mortgaged property. The most critical aspect of ownership is the right of disposition. Once Li Shuai obtained the notarized power of attorney, he effectively replaced Ge Liang's right to dispose of the property. Xiao Zhongxiang effectively also had the rights of the owner of the property. When Ge Liang failed to repay the loan as agreed, Xiao Zhongxiang could transfer the mortgaged property at any time without negotiating with Ge Liang. Therefore, Ge Liang's act of simultaneously executing the loan contract and issuing a power of attorney, promising to fully authorize Li Shuai to sell the property upon default, is analogous to a lien waiver clause (liupa tiaokuan) and should be deemed invalid. The court did not accept the arguments of the Defendant and the Third Parties that the agency procedures were lawfully established and valid.

Second, there was malicious collusion between Third Party Li Shuai and Defendant Li Hui in entering into the housing sales contract. Considering the relationships among the parties and the process of entering into and performing the relevant contracts, Defendant and Li Shuai are biological brothers. Li Shuai and Xiao Zhongxiang had previously acted as agents in the sale of properties. Even if the power of attorney permitted the agent to sign a contract with anyone, in this case, Defendant had been involved since the date Plaintiff Ge Liang borrowed the money, entering into the first housing sales contract with Plaintiff. Defendant knew that the disputed property was mortgaged and involved a debt relationship, and that there were actual residents with household registration. When he later entered into the housing sales contract with the Third Party, no provisions were made for key transaction aspects and routine matters such as the time for vacating the property, delayed vacating, delayed payment, how to discharge the mortgage, or how to handle the household registration. This clearly defied common sense. The Defendant and the Third Parties also did not provide evidence of paying the corresponding purchase price. Considering the case as a whole, the Defendant and the Third Parties had prior consultations, made loans to the Plaintiff, and subsequently cooperated with each other. Without consulting the Plaintiff, relying on the power of attorney previously issued by the Plaintiff, they directly transferred the mortgaged property used as security for repayment. To a certain extent, this harmed the Plaintiff's legitimate rights and interests. The above conduct of the Defendant and the Third Parties cannot escape the suspicion of malicious collusion. The court did not accept the arguments of the Defendant and the Third Parties that the Plaintiff had long been aware of the relationships and roles of the Defendant and the Third Parties and that there was no malicious collusion.

Finally, the power of attorney issued by Plaintiff Ge Liang was an invalid civil juristic act due to lack of genuine expression of intent. Third Party Xiao Zhongxiang, through Third Party Li Shuai, directly transferred the mortgaged property to Defendant Li Hui. This realization of the debt through private means does not comply with the provisions of the Property Law and the Security Law regarding the exercise of mortgage rights, nor does it align with the true expression of the parties' intentions. A civil juristic act is a civil act that meets general validity requirements and is lawful. The default rule is that a legal act takes effect according to the parties' expression of intent. The expression of intent must be genuine; this is a substantive requirement for a civil juristic act. Otherwise, it is an invalid civil juristic act. Although the title to the disputed property was registered in Plaintiff's name, the property was actually occupied long-term by the family of Hou Xuejing, Plaintiff's cousin. Ge Liang borrowed money from Xiao Zhongxiang and simultaneously issued a power of attorney to Li Shuai authorizing him to sell the disputed property in Ge Liang's name. This was essentially an act to guarantee the realization of Xiao Zhongxiang's claim. The true intention was to obtain a loan, not to sell the disputed property. At the same time, Xiao Zhongxiang took advantage of Ge Liang's urgent need for funds, compelling Ge Liang to accommodate her wishes and reluctantly issue a notarized power of attorney to Li Shuai for the sale of the disputed property. It is difficult to say that this was done out of Ge Liang's own free will. Therefore, the civil act by which Ge Liang issued the power of attorney granting Li Shuai the authority to sign the real estate sales contract, collect the purchase price, and handle property title transfer procedures, lacked the general validity requirement of genuine expression of intent and should be deemed invalid. The court did not accept the arguments of the Defendant and the Third Parties that the Plaintiff's authorization to sell the disputed property was his true expression of intent.

In summary, the real estate sales contract entered into by Third Party Li Shuai in the name of Plaintiff Ge Liang with Defendant Li Hui is a contract that conceals an illegal purpose under a lawful form. It violates legal prohibitions, is not a true expression of Plaintiff's intention, does not meet the validity requirements for a civil juristic act, and should be deemed void under the law. After the contract is confirmed void, Defendant shall restore the title of the disputed property to Ge Liang's name, and the mortgage right of Xiao Zhongxiang on the property shall be reinstated. As for the loan and mortgage contract dispute between Ge Liang and Xiao Zhongxiang, it does not fall within the scope of this case. The parties may resolve it through negotiation or through separate legal proceedings.

Accordingly, the Yangpu District People's Court of Shanghai, in accordance with Article 55 of the General Principles of the Civil Law of the People's Republic of China, Article 52, paragraphs (2), (3), and (5), and Article 58 of the Contract Law of the People's Republic of China, Article 186 and Article 195 of the Property Law of the People's Republic of China, and Article 40 and Article 53 of the Security Law of the People's Republic of China, rendered judgment on September 20, 2016, as follows:

1. The "Shanghai Real Estate Sales Contract" (Contract No. 2211220) entered into by Third Party Li Shuai in the name of Ge Liang with Li Hui is void;
2. Defendant Li Hui shall, within thirty days from the effective date of this judgment, assist Plaintiff Ge Liang in restoring the title of the property located at Room ×-×, Building ×, Shiguang Yicun, Yangpu District, Shanghai to Ge Liang's name;
3. Plaintiff Ge Liang shall, within thirty days from the effective date of this judgment, assist Third Party Xiao Zhongxiang in restoring the mortgage registration, establishing a mortgage right on the property at Room ×-×, Building ×, Shiguang Yicun, Yangpu District, Shanghai with Xiao Zhongxiang as the mortgagee and the amount of the secured claim being RMB 1,200,000.

Li Hui, dissatisfied with the judgment of first instance, appealed to the Shanghai No. 2 Intermediate People's Court, alleging: Hou Xuejing did not repay the loan on behalf of the appellee Ge Liang; rather, Hou Xuejing borrowed money in the appellee's name and was the actual borrower. Currently, the appellant Li Hui resides in one room of the disputed house, and leases out another room. The appellee, with a genuine intention to sell the house, voluntarily entered into the "Shanghai Real Estate Sales Contract" for the disputed house with the appellant, and, to ensure the smooth performance of the contract, voluntarily granted Li Shuai the authority to sign the real estate sales contract, collect the purchase price, and handle the procedures for transfer of title. The appellee's above actions have no necessary connection with Xiao Zhongxiang's lending of money to him. Therefore, this case does not involve any act of "the third party selling the house to realize the creditor's rights." The actual seller of the house was not Li Shuai but the appellee himself, and this has no relation whatsoever to Xiao Zhongxiang. The above "Shanghai Real Estate Sales Contract" does not contain any grounds for invalidity, nor does it involve any illegal acts such as fraud or duress, and it certainly does not harm national or public interests. The appellee knew from the outset that the appellant and Li Shuai were brothers and was fully aware of the legal relationships among the parties and could have foreseen the legal consequences of his actions. The court of first instance erred and acted hastily in finding that the signing of the disputed sales contract constituted malicious collusion solely on the ground that the appellant and Li Shuai were brothers. The sales contract for the disputed house was concluded in October 2014, and the transaction procedures were carried out in April 2015. However, the court of first instance used only the real estate market price at the end of April 2015 as a reference and concluded that the appellee's grant of authority was an invalid civil act due to lack of genuine expression of intent. This basis is unreasonable and does not accord with the facts of this case. In summary, it is often a party that fails to keep its word that asserts the invalidity of a contract, seeking to recover a house that is constantly appreciating in value through a declaration of invalidity. If the appellee's claims in the first instance were upheld, it would seriously harm the appellant's interests and undermine the principle of good faith. On these grounds, the appellant contends that the original judgment found the facts unclearly and misapplied the law, and requests the court to vacate it in accordance with the law, remand the case for retrial, or amend the judgment to dismiss the appellee's claims in the first instance.

The appellee, Ge Liang, argued: Because he was unable to repay the loan and Hou Xuejing's family resided in the disputed house, Hou Xuejing repaid part of the loan on his behalf to secure her continued residence. Currently, after being evicted from the disputed house, the appellee does not know who resides or uses the house. To realize the prohibited pactum commissorium, the appellant Li Hui, in coordination with Li Shuai, Xiao Zhongxiang, and others, sold the disputed house, which clearly violates mandatory legal provisions. The series of powers of attorney, house sale contracts, etc. signed by the appellee to obtain the loan were intended to enable Xiao Zhongxiang to ultimately realize his creditor's rights. The original judgment correctly found that the appellant, Li Shuai, Xiao Zhongxiang, and others acted in malicious collusion, and that their sale of the disputed house violated mandatory legal provisions and was therefore invalid. The appellant is not a bona fide purchaser. The appreciation of the house is unrelated to the appellant. The appellee's borrowing created a creditor-debtor relationship, and he is willing to repay the loan. It was the appellant who rejected the mediation proposal during the first instance proceedings. Given that the appellee had no genuine intention to sell the disputed house, the original judgment found the facts clearly and correctly applied the law. The appellee requests the court to affirm the judgment in accordance with the law.

The third party at first instance, Li Shuai, stated: He agreed with the appellant Li Hui's arguments on appeal and requested the court to uphold the appellant's appeal in accordance with the law.

The third party at first instance, Xiao Zhongxiang, stated: He agreed with the appellant Li Hui's arguments on appeal and requested the court to uphold the appellant's appeal in accordance with the law.

After trial at second instance, the Shanghai No. 2 Intermediate People's Court confirmed the facts found in the first instance.

The Shanghai No. 2 Intermediate People's Court held on second instance:

A party has the burden of providing evidence to prove the facts on which its claims are based or to rebut the facts on which the opposing party's claims are based. If no evidence is provided or the evidence is insufficient to prove the party's factual assertions, the party bearing the burden of proof shall bear the adverse consequences. The appellant Li Hui's assertion that Hou Xuejing borrowed money in the name of the appellee Ge Liang and was the actual borrower, lacking sufficient supporting evidence, cannot be accepted by the court. Although the parties concerned, regarding the relevant creditor's rights and agency, obtained notarized documents, and Li Shuai, acting on the notarized power of attorney, sold the disputed house on behalf of the appellee Ge Liang, the court of first instance found that in the "Shanghai Real Estate Sales Contract" for the disputed house, the clauses concerning key and routine matters of the house transaction were left blank and not agreed upon. Additionally, when the appellee and Xiao Zhongxiang signed the mortgage loan contract, they simultaneously signed the corresponding sales contract, and obtained a creditor's document with enforceability and a notarized power of attorney. The aforesaid mortgage contract did not stipulate that if the loan could not be repaid at maturity, the mortgaged disputed house would become the property of Xiao Zhongxiang. Therefore, the legal relationship between the appellee and Xiao Zhongxiang was one of loan. The appellee's mortgaging of the disputed house was merely to secure the repayment of the loan. The original judgment correctly found that the appellee had no genuine intention to sell the house, and the court of second instance affirms this finding. In light of the signing dates of the relevant documents and the facts found, the court of first instance held that if a mortgage contract stipulates that upon the maturity of the debt and the mortgagee's failure to receive payment, the ownership of the mortgaged property shall be transferred to the mortgagee, such a stipulation is invalid, which is consistent with legal provisions. The court of first instance's finding that the appellee's issuance of the power of attorney, granting Li Shuai the authority to sign the real estate sales contract, collect the purchase price, handle title transfer procedures, etc., was a civil act lacking the essential element of genuine expression of intent and therefore invalid, was not improper. The appellant's claims on appeal, lacking sufficient factual and legal basis, cannot be supported by the court of second instance.

In summary, the facts of the first instance were clearly found and the judgment was not improper. Accordingly, the Shanghai No. 2 Intermediate People's Court, pursuant to Article 170, Paragraph 1, Item (1) of the Civil Procedure Law of the People's Republic of China, rendered the following judgment on January 18, 2017:

Appeal dismissed. The original judgment is affirmed.

This judgment is final.
